Article Title: Toll rises to 31 as 22-hour standoff ends at Pakistan police line HQ
Article Text:
What began on Friday as a suicide blast at the compound’s perimeter gate rapidly developed into an active siege

NEW DELHI: The death toll from the attack on the police lines headquarters in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, rose to at least 31, with over 100 injured, as military and police forces concluded the 22-hour-long stand-off Saturday noon.What began on Friday as a suicide blast at the compound's perimeter gate rapidly developed into an active siege after at least seven operatives from the Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP) group breached the counter terrorism department (CTD) and intelligence facilities. In a turn of events, the operatives, once inside, managed to reach the facility's weapons depot, released many detained terror suspects, and armed some of them to fight the Pakistani personnel, sources said.Despite a large deployment, heavy gunfire was exchanged through Friday night and Saturday morning. A military command with the infantry division was used to direct the Pak govt's operation, but strong resistance from inside the lockdown zone prolonged the multi-building standoff, leaving scores wounded and critical.Among those killed were SP Akbar Shinwari, a deputy SP and Dr Israel Orakzai, head of the pediatrics department at Kohat hospital.A few civilians also died in the exchange of fire.Special Service Group (SSG) Zarrar unit and infantry division had to be pressed into service to end the siege and clear the compound. Khyber Police claimed to have neutralised eight of the attackers. The facility, which has been facilitating establishment of new terror camps in KPK region, was struck Friday afternoon with a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device (VBIED), enabling multiple suicide attackers to force their way inside the premises shooting indiscriminately.
Article Summary: The death toll from the attack on the police lines headquarters in kohat, khyber pakhtunkhwa, rose to at least 31. Over 100 injured, as military and police forces concluded the 22-hour-long stand-off saturday noon.what began on friday as a suicide blast at the compound’s perimeter gate rapidly developed into an active siege.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday inaugurated a two-day international conference on “The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics”, organised by the National Green Tribunal (NGT) at Vigyan Bhawan in New Delhi.The conference, being held on September 19 and 20, brings together judges, environmental experts, senior government officials and representatives of various environmental and judicial institutions from India and abroad. Judicial representatives from 17 countries are also participating in the event.Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant, Union Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Bhupender Yadav, Attorney General R Venkataramani and NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava attended the inaugural session.The conference will feature four technical sessions focusing on key environmental and climate-related issues. According to the NGT, the discussions will examine major challenges facing the world, identify gaps in policy-making and implementation, and explore ways to strengthen institutional cooperation.The event also aims to facilitate the exchange of successful environmental practices and strengthen environmental justice amid growing challenges linked to climate change, development and governance.President Droupadi Murmu will attend the valedictory session on Sunday. Union minister Manohar Lal, Supreme Court judge Justice PS Narasimha, NGT Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and Solicitor General Tushar Mehta are also scheduled to attend the concluding session.The conference is expected to work towards developing a roadmap for addressing present and future environmental and climate challenges.

A Sri Lankan opposition lawmaker on Saturday urged President Anura Kumara Dissanayake to seek Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s intervention in the case of a young Sri Lankan Tamil facing judicial proceedings in Saudi Arabia.In making the appeal, Mano Ganesan, a leader of the Tamil Progressive Alliance, cited PM Modi’s “close ties” with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman.“I urge President @anuradisanayake to bring #Anojan_Sivarasa’s desperate plight to the urgent attention of your friend, recipient of ‘SriLanka Rathna’ Prime Minister Narendra Modi,” Ganesan wrote on X.“Given PM Modi’s close ties with Saudi Prime Minister and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, I appeal to you to ask PM Modi to personally intervene with Crown Prince Salman and seek a humanitarian resolution for Anojan,” he added.The appeal concerns Sri Lankan national Anojan Sivarasa, whose family has claimed that he was sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia over a social media post allegedly amounting to blasphemy.Sri Lanka’s foreign ministry, however, has not confirmed that Sivarasa has been sentenced to death.Sivarasa, a minority Tamil from Sri Lanka’s Eastern Province, is a resident of Natpittimunai in Kalmunai. He travelled to Saudi Arabia for employment nine months ago.The Sri Lankan ministry of foreign affairs on Friday confirmed that it remains engaged with Saudi authorities over the case.“The ministry remains engaged with the relevant Saudi authorities through diplomatic channels and is taking appropriate steps to safeguard Mr. Anojan Sivarasa’s interests and provide him with all possible assistance,” it said.Sivarasa was initially sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi riyals after being found guilty of posting social media content deemed insulting to a religion.According to the report, his lawyer later verbally informed the Sri Lankan Embassy in Riyadh that the sentence had reportedly been enhanced to capital punishment.The embassy, however, is awaiting the formal written judgment from Saudi judicial authorities before confirming the development.The lawyer has also informed the embassy that the judgment could be appealed before Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court within one month. Article Title: 'I knew this was the end of my career': Ajit Doval recalls when his agents were captured by China
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Saturday recalled one of the most difficult moments of his early career, when a group of operatives sent across the border went missing and were later found to be in Chinese custody.Speaking as the chief guest at the two-day convocation ceremony of IIT Roorkee, NSA Doval said he was deeply worried after receiving no information about the group's whereabouts.He said: “We got no reports of any avalanche or anything. It was a matter of deep worry and concern. But I got a telephone call from the headquarters, and my boss told me, "Have you sent some people across?" I said, "I do not know. They must be coming. They should have come in five or six days, but now it is about ten or eleven days." He said, "They are in Chinese custody now." They were caught by the Chinese and interrogated. Anyway, the Chinese returned them, probably after some talks or negotiations, or a deal must have been struck. So, they returned totally shattered, in shambles. And an inquiry was started. I knew that this was the end of my career. I was still in my twenties, and I had to start a new career.I saw the incident as something very unprofessional.”Doval said an inquiry was later conducted and he was not held responsible for the incident.“Anyway, the inquiry was over. I wasn't found at fault. Probably, I had done everything right. The sketches and the maps that were given to us by the headquarters had some defects and mistakes in them. That is how it happened," the NSA added.He also spoke about the opportunities available to today's younger generation, particularly with rapid advances in technology."You may not be conscious of the fact that in the last 1000 years, you are the luckiest generation, which is going to have so many opportunities. Generations before you were struggling under slavery. They did not have those opportunities which opened up for you. And not only that, things have changed here, but globally things have changed for the better for you... You are coming at an age when technology will be the most important driving factor in any country's or society's growth and progress," Ajit Doval said.The two-day convocation began at IIT Roorkee on Saturday, with degrees set to be awarded to 2,701 students. NSA Doval attended the event as the chief guest.
Article Summary: Ajit doval recalls china custody episode: ‘i knew this was the end of my career’ nsa doval said he was deeply worried after receiving no information about the group's whereabouts. He was speaking as the chief guest at the two-day convocation ceremony of iit roorkee.

Article Title: PM Modi pushes back on West’s narrative over carbon emissions
Article Text:
PM Modi being presented a memento during ‘The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics’, at Vigyan Bhawan, in New Delhi Saturday

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi Saturday questioned the narrative in which the responsibility for carbon emissions is pinned on developing countries while Western countries are absolved of their role as historical polluters, even as he reaffirmed the country’s commitment to climate action and stressed that it has the best record among G20 countries. “In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than India’s... India presents this fact strongly on global platforms... We are establishing new benchmarks for environmental protection by taking the world along,” he said. His remarks at an international conference on ‘The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics’, organised by NGT, come as the world gears up for the global climate conference scheduled for Nov in Turkiye.He said India is providing solutions to modern climate challenges even as its per capita carbon emissions are less than half of the global average.The PM’s remarks are being seen as a pushback against the West’s attempt, despite its historical responsibility for alarming emission levels, to suggest that India needs to accept stiff emission-reduction targets. India’s cumulative (1751-2024) contribution to overall carbon emissions is merely 3.5%, compared with 23.5% for US, 15.4% for China, 6.6% for Russia, 5.1% for Germany, and 4.3% for UK.Though India is currently the third-largest emitter, its per capita emission, as Modi underlined, at 2.2 tonnes per person per year, is less than half of the global average (4.7 tonnes per person per year) and six times less than the per capita emission of US (14.2 tonnes) and Russia (14 tonnes).India has always raised these points at all multilateral forums, pointing to equity and importance of a cut in emissions by big polluters who developed by burning fossil fuels over the past two centuries, which led to global warming. India, however, has never deviated from its responsibility and has fulfilled climate action pledges under the Paris Agreement.“India is the only country in G20 that has fulfilled all the commitments it made at the COP21 summit in Paris (in 2015), and has done so ahead of schedule. This is the strength of ‘Hindustan’ that I am talking about. On every parameter — non-fossil fuel, solar energy capacity, curbing carbon emissions — India’s performance is today a subject of positive discussion worldwide,” said PM Modi while urging the gathering of jurists, academicians, policymakers, scientists, environmental experts and other stakeholders from 17 countries across the world to look at the figures.Looking ahead to COP31, scheduled for Nov in Antalya, Turkey, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav said India will continue to advocate climate action centred on equity, implementation and the needs of vulnerable countries.
Article Summary: Pm narendra modi questioned the narrative in which responsibility for carbon emissions is pinned on developing countries while western countries are absolved of their role as historical polluters. His remarks at an international conference on ‘the future of environment and climate dynamics’, organised by ngt, come as the world gears up for the global climate conference scheduled for nov.

Article Title: ‘Resist him forcefully’: Congress hits back at Trump over Russia sanctions law
Article Text:
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh

NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday said the only way to counter a “bully” was to “resist him forcefully”, after US president Donald Trump signed into law a legislation expanding sanctions on Russia and Iran and giving Washington new tariff powers targeting major buyers of Russian energy.AICC general secretary Jairam Ramesh made the remarks in a post on X after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Friday. The White House said the law authorises and expands sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran.“The only way to counter a bully is to resist him forcefully,” Ramesh said.The legislation gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from countries that meet specified criteria linked to purchases of Russian crude oil or natural gas and sanctions evasion. It also targets Russian officials, financial institutions, defence networks and the country’s so-called “shadow fleet”.The measure does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on any specific country, with the law giving Trump discretion over its implementation.Earlier on Wednesday, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said the threat of up to 100 per cent US tariffs on Indian goods showed the government’s foreign and trade policies had “miserably failed”.He said, “The threat of up to 100 per cent US tariffs on Indian goods shows how the Modi govt's foreign and trade policies have miserably failed.” Kharge also claimed the government had agreed to a trade framework expanding US access to Indian agriculture, alleging it “mortgag[ed] the interests of our farmers”.The legislation comes as India continues to face questions over its purchases of Russian energy. The ministry of external affairs said New Delhi’s energy sourcing decisions are guided by national interest.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal earlier said meeting the requirements of India’s 1.4 billion people remained an “imperative”.“When it comes to energy sourcing, it is based on our national interest. We have said that meeting the energy requirements of our 1.4 billion people is an imperative that we have to follow. And we continue to buy energy from diversified sources,” Jaiswal said.On the new US law, Jaiswal said India had already conveyed its concerns to senior levels of the US administration.“As we have stated, at senior levels of the US administration, we have conveyed the implications that this legislation could have on India's energy security, for international energy markets, and for the overall bilateral relationship. I don't have anything further to add at this point,” he said.The White House said Trump signed the legislation on September 18. The law extends the Iran Sanctions Act for five years and expands measures against Russia’s energy and financial sectors.
Article Summary: Congress general secretary jairam ramesh said the only way to counter a bully is to resist him forcefully. Trump signed the lindsey o. graham sanctioning russia and iran act of 2026 on friday. The law authorises and expands sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions on russia and extends existing sanctions on iran.

NEW DELHI: Former vice president Mohammad Hamid Ansari on Saturday cited former prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru 's remarks about the “danger to India” while referring to concerns raised by late constitutional expert and author AG Noorani in his book The RSS : A Menace to India.He was addressing the event, titled “Remembering a Polymath: The Life and Times of Abdul Ghafoor Noorani”, organised at the India Islamic Cultural Centre to commemorate the life and works of the jurist and author.Addressing an event, Ansari recalled jurist and author Abdul Ghafoor Noorani's observations in the introduction to his 2019 book and cited remarks by Nehru that were recorded by former Foreign Secretary Jagat Singh Gundevia during a meeting of Ministry of External Affairs officials.‘The RSS: A Menace to India’ was the title of the book published in 2019. The opening lines of the introduction, where A.G. Noorani used a couplet, reflected what he described as the prevailing sentiment among Muslims in India today. He also referred to Noorani's criticism of what he saw as a shift from civic nationalism towards cultural nationalism.“In recent years, we have experienced the emergence of trends and practices that dispute the well-established principle of civic nationalism and interpose a new and imaginary practice of cultural nationalism,” Ansari said.“It seeks to present an electoral majority in the guise of a religious majority and monopolise political power. It wants to distinguish citizens based on their faith, give vent to intolerance, insinuate otherness, and promote disquiet and insecurity,” he added.Ansari raised concerns over what he described as emerging trends that challenge the principle of civic nationalism.During his speech, Ansari said, “Some of its recent manifestations are chilling and reflect poorly on our claim to be governed by the rule of law. It’s a question that has to be answered. These trends need to be contested and contested legally and contested politically.”Reacting to Ansari's remarks, the BJP Scheduled Tribe Morcha said the statement brought what it described as Congress's “anti-Hindu politics” into focus. Article Title: Houthis, Saudis, Iran - and the future of Middle Eastern oil
Article Text:
Houthi fighters stand in front of what they say is a downed Saudi jet, at a location given as Yemen

What’s the latest Houthi offensive all about?

Why is this a serious headache?

Why now?

Why are Saudis in a jam?

What are the takeaways?

In a lightning offensive last week, Yemen’s Houthis took over much of the country’s Red Sea coast, threatening shipping in the vital sea lane that had emerged as an alternative to Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. Houthis have been fighting a Saudi-led military coalition for a decade, although a 2022 UN-brokered truce halted their attacks on Saudi territory. But the Houthis’ latest move has once again sent oil prices north of the $100 per barrel mark, adding another front to the wider US-Israel war against Iran. Here’s the lowdown on why the Houthis’ Red Sea threat matters, how this puts Saudi Arabia in a serious pickle, and what it means for the Iran war:The offensive saw Houthis take over key parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. This adds weight to the Houthi threat to shipping in the vital sea lane. In fact, Houthis had earlier declared a blockade of Saudi ships in the region. Now they can seriously enforce this. Their mere presence along the coastline will make shippers jittery and raise insurance costs.With Strait of Hormuz effectively locked up by Iran and US, Red Sea had emerged as a vital alternative route, especially for energy trade out of the region.Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was working at full capacity, transporting around 7 million barrels of oil daily across the breadth of the peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. This was a crucial lifeline for the global energy trade that had been severely restricted following the outbreak of the Iran war in Feb. But that East-West pipeline was hit by a drone attack last week — blamed on Iran-backed Shia militias in Iraq — to coincide with the Houthi advance on the Red Sea coast. Both operations seem to have been coordinated to put the choke on Red Sea shipping, which has to pass through the narrow Bab el-Mandeb strait that Houthis can now theoretically shut down.The timing of all this is not a coincidence. Actually, when the Iran war began, among Iran’s proxies in the region, Houthis held back. But in July, following the state funeral of Iran’s former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, an Iranian plane carrying the Houthi delegation back to Yemen was threatened by Saudi Arabia. Riyadh did not want that plane to land, and bombed the airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital of Sanaa. But that plane landed anyway.Following the episode, Houthi rhetoric against the Saudis flared up. But the key development that may have pushed Houthis into action could be the American blockade of Iranian ports and shipping in Persian Gulf.By many estimates, that blockade appears to be working, and putting enormous pressure on the Iranian economy. Tehran is unable to push out its own oil, the Iranian rial has tanked, and Iranians have actually taken to saving eggs instead of hard cash. Plus, this is a strategy that plays into America’s strength — it can carry out a naval blockade for a far longer period than a continuous kinetic war against Iran.So, Iran, through the Houthi action, is sending the message that if oil can’t pass through Hormuz, any alternative routes, including through the Red Sea, will also be shut. In short, the energy trade in the region is handcuffed till the war is resolved.What do Houthis want? The Houthis’ main grievance is against the Saudis, whom they have been fighting since 2015. But, of course, as a member of Iran’s so-called ‘Axis of Resistance’, they are now being heavily supported by Tehran in terms of material and intelligence inputs. Especially since the Gaza and Iran wars have seen Tehran’s two main proxies in Hezbollah and Hamas take a huge battering. So, the Iranian Axis appears to be undergoing a recalibration, with Houthis and Iran-backed militias in Iraq taking a more leading role among the proxies. Ultimately Houthis want legitimacy. Their attacks against Saudi Arabia — they reportedly fired a drone at Mecca earlier this week — raise their profile. Their capture of the Red Sea coast gives them international attention. And these, in turn, see them emerge as the primary force in Yemen, instead of the internationally backed Yemeni transition govt. Obviously, all of this helps Iran.Because US has refused to directly intervene against Houthis this time. Washington is providing diplomatic and advisory support to Riyadh, but not much else. Saudis want missile and drone interceptors. But US stocks are running low, thanks to its war with Iran. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has similarly sought assistance from Egypt and UK. But no one is rushing military aid to Riyadh. Interestingly, even the recently inked Mecca Pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan hasn’t been activated.First, Houthis prove Iran’s Axis of Resistance is changing shape, with the Yemini militia taking a leading role. This has implications for both the Iran war, and security in Red Sea and Horn of Africa region. And second, alternative routes to Hormuz for energy transit, whether through sea or pipelines, are also not fully secure. They can be targeted by a host of Iran-backed militias in the region. This puts West Asia’s dominance in global energy supply under a serious cloud, perhaps forcing the international community to look for alternatives away from the region.
Article Summary: Yemen's houthis took over much of the country's red sea coast, threatening shipping. Red sea had emerged as an alternative to strait of hormuz in persian gulf. Houthis have been fighting a saudi-led military coalition for a decade. Move has once again sent oil prices north of the $100 per barrel mark.

NEW DELHI: Air India Express suspended eight crew members for three months for failing to complete the mandatory post-flight declaration, news agency ANI reported, citing sources.The incident took place on August 2 after the flight landed in Amritsar from Dubai.According to ANI, the crew was required to undergo the post-flight declaration within two hours of landing. However, they were delayed by 35 minutes and submitted the declaration after two hours and 35 minutes."As per the airline’s mandatory rules for testing of psychoactive substances, all crew members underwent the test, and the reports came negative," sources told ANI."The entire incident was reported to the DGCA, and the airline decided to suspend the eight crew members for three months," they added.According to DGCA rules, crew members operating international flights for Indian carriers must complete a post-flight alcohol test within two hours of landing in India, regardless of individual circumstances during that window.

The couple had bought the Italian-style villa in 2007, around the time David Beckham moved to the US to play for LA Galaxy. Property records and reports put their purchase price at about $18.2 million, meaning the sale brought them nearly $15 million more before taxes, fees and other costs. The deal was completed off-market, with the buyer listed through a limited liability company, keeping the new owner’s identity private.David Beckham and Victoria Beckham bought the Beverly Hills property in 2007 after David moved to Los Angeles to begin his Major League Soccer career with LA Galaxy. The home was an Italian villa-style property tucked away behind large gates and a private drive.The purchase price is one area where different reports have given different numbers. The Los Angeles Times reported that the Beckhams paid $18.2 million for the house. Other websites have since repeated a $22 million figure, but the $18.2 million figure is the one backed by the 2018 property reporting from the Los Angeles Times.The house gave the family a private base in Los Angeles while David played in the US. Victoria Beckham was also building her career outside football, first through fashion and later through her own clothing label.The property had about 11,500 to more than 13,000 square feet of living space, depending on the source. It had six bedrooms, multiple living areas, a library, an elevator and a media and music room. The house was also surrounded by gates and landscaping that gave the family a high level of privacy.The size of the home was only part of what made it notable. Its layout was designed for a large family and for entertaining, with several rooms spread across the property.The villa had six bedrooms and about nine to 10 bathrooms, with reports differing slightly on the exact bathroom count. There was also a library, a media and music room, formal living and dining spaces and an elevator.Outside, the property had a swimming pool and large private grounds. Its position behind iron gates and at the end of a private drive meant visitors could not simply see the house from the street.The home also became closely linked with the Beckham family’s years in Los Angeles. Their children lived there during the family’s time in the city, while David continued his football career and Victoria worked on her growing fashion business.The house was not simply a short-term stop after David’s move to the US. The couple kept it for more than a decade, even after David’s playing career in Los Angeles had ended.By the time the house was sold, the family’s life had changed considerably. David Beckham retired from professional football in 2013, while Victoria Beckham’s fashion business had become an increasingly important part of her career in London.The family also had a growing connection to the UK, where they had a home in Holland Park and a country property in the Cotswolds. Their children were also spending more of their time in Britain.David’s business interests later brought the family closer to Miami. He became a co-owner of Inter Miami CF, giving him another major reason to spend time in South Florida.That made the Beverly Hills property less central to the family’s life. Instead of putting it through a traditional public listing, the Beckhams sold it privately.The Los Angeles Times reported in October 2018 that the house had been sold off-market for about $33.1 million. The buyer appeared in property records through a limited liability company, so the identity of the person or people behind the purchase was not publicly disclosed.The private sale also meant there was no long public listing process for the house. The deal was completed in September 2018, after the Beckhams had owned the property for about 11 years.Using the reported $18.2 million purchase price and the roughly $33.1 million sale price, the Beckhams made about $14.9 million in gross profit on the property before transaction costs, taxes, renovations and other expenses.The sale therefore represented a rise of roughly 82% in the property’s price over the 11-year holding period, although that does not mean the couple took home the full increase as profit.Mansion Global also reported that the home had been quietly shopped around before the eventual transaction and confirmed that it was sold without being publicly listed. The buyer was recorded as a Delaware limited liability company.The Beverly Hills sale also fits into a wider change in the Beckhams’ US property interests. In 2020, David and Victoria bought a full-floor residence at Miami’s One Thousand Museum for $19.8 million. The Zaha Hadid-designed tower became part of their South Florida property holdings during David’s growing involvement with Inter Miami.That Miami apartment was later sold for about $24.6 million in 2026, according to property reporting. The couple also bought a waterfront Miami Beach mansion in 2024 for about $72.3 million, below its $80 million asking price.So, while the Beverly Hills home is now part of the Beckhams’ past property portfolio, its sale marked an important point in the family’s move away from their old Los Angeles base and toward a stronger connection with Miami.
Article Summary: David and victoria beckham bought the beverly hills property in 2007 after david moved to los angeles to begin his major league soccer career. The home was an italian villa-style property tucked away behind large gates and a private drive. It had six bedrooms, multiple living areas, a library, an elevator and a media and music room.

Article Title: 'Negotiate or face decisive war': Iran conveys terms to US for restarting talks, sets 7 conditions
Article Text:
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei laid out the conditions that Iran sent to the US

Iran has formally conveyed its conditions to United States for ending the war, with its top official saying it has set out seven conditions for restarting negotiations while warning that it is also prepared for a “decisive war”.Iran’s supreme national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview that Qatar had passed Tehran’s conditions to Washington and that Iran was awaiting US President Donald Trump’s response. “Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade,” Rezaei said.“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions. Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” he added.In a separate post on X, he confirmed that it had announced seven conditions for starting negotiations with the US, saying Washington would have to accept Iran’s “rights and conditions” if it wanted to “escape the quagmire” and avoid becoming further entangled in the conflict.“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions.Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” Rezaei added.Meanwhile, Rezaei also told Al Jazeera that Iran was also preparing for the possibility of another US strike, describing it as “very much on the cards”. He said Tehran had changed its military planning and was now focused on US naval assets across the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.He claimed Iran had recently test-fired a multi-warhead anti-ship missile near a US vessel or aircraft carrier and warned that any future Iranian response would include US bases and American commercial interests in the region.At the same time, Rezaei said Tehran was pursuing diplomacy to bring the conflict to an end “as soon as possible”. Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to restart negotiations between Washington and Tehran after their earlier memorandum of understanding expired.On the nuclear issue, Rezaei said Iran had not decided to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, although he warned that further sanctions or a referral of its nuclear file to the UN Security Council “may push Tehran into withdrawing”.He also said Tehran remained open to an agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, saying the two sides had come within “a short step” of reaching a deal before it was shelved.The comments come as Washington weighs its next move in the conflict. Trump told Axios this week that he was facing a “big decision” over whether to resume major military action against Iran. “Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not?” Trump had said, adding, “Anything could happen with me.”
Article Summary: Iran's security chief mohsen rezaei laid out the conditions that iran sent to the us. He said qatar had passed tehran’s conditions to washington and that iran was awaiting us president donald trump's response. “our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and anend to the naval blockade,” he said.

Article Title: Meet Joe Petraro-Hyppolite: 13-year-old New York boy who scored 1,590 on SAT and is set to pursue a master's at NYU, with a reported IQ of 168
Article Text:
Image: CBS News

Joe Petraro-Hyppolite’s remarkable academic journey

Teenager discusses learning and reported IQ of 168

Image: CBS News

His mother recalls his earlier educational experience

Volunteering and ambitions beyond university

Joe Petraro-Hyppolite, a 13-year-old from Long Island, New York, is preparing to begin a master's programme at New York University in 2027. His academic journey has attracted attention after he reportedly scored 1,590 out of 1,600 on the SAT at the age of 10 and earned his high school diploma at 11. He is currently working towards an undergraduate degree and plans to graduate in May 2027. Joe has an IQ of 168 and has also attended Louisiana State University. His planned master's programme will focus on sports management, while kinesiology and biology are among his other academic interests. Alongside his education, he volunteers at a nursing home and hopes to become a palaeontologist.His unusually accelerated education has allowed him to explore university-level subjects years earlier than most students, while his varied interests span science, athletics and healthcare. He has also spoken about continuing to balance academic study with community involvement and long-term career ambitions.Petraro-Hyppolite achieved several academic milestones at an unusually young age. He scored 1,590 on the SAT at 10 and received his high school diploma at 11. He later attended Louisiana State University and continued working towards his undergraduate degree alongside considerably older students.His academic progress has allowed him to pursue university education during his early teens. The SAT has a maximum score of 1,600, placing his reported result 10 points below the highest possible score.Petraro-Hyppolite told CBS News New York that he had been accepted into a master's programme at New York University and planned to begin in 2027. He said his master's would be in sports management and also mentioned kinesiology and biology. He is expected to complete his undergraduate degree in May 2027 before starting postgraduate studies at NYU. Petraro-Hyppolite's path stands out not only for how quickly he has advanced, but also for the clear direction he has set for a future career in sports and health.Petraro-Hyppolite has spoken about his learning process and the effort involved in managing an accelerated academic journey. Despite his reported IQ of 168, he said that he still needs to study and understand material before retaining it. “It’s not like I was shot out the womb knowing everything I know. I have to learn it once or twice. Then I’ll know,” he said. Joe also described feeling nervous and excited about the next stage of his education, as he prepares to take on new academic challenges. Even with his remarkable record, his story is a reminder that steady effort, not effortless genius, lies behind each of his achievements.His mother, Anne Petraro-Hyppolite, said her son's progress was particularly meaningful because he had previously been placed in special education classes after being diagnosed with Tourette syndrome. The condition is a neurological disorder associated with motor and vocal tics. Speaking about her son's achievements, she said, “It's just surreal. When he graduated high school so young, it was surreal, but this is . .. everything he does is surreal. He just loves to learn. He is like a sponge.”Alongside his studies, Petraro-Hyppolite volunteers at a nursing home in the Five Towns area of Long Island, where he helps residents. Although he plans to pursue a master's in sports management, Joe has also expressed an ambition to become a palaeontologist in the future. His interests extend across sports, biology and prehistoric life. For now, he is focused on completing his undergraduate degree in May 2027 and preparing for postgraduate education at NYU.
Article Summary: Joe petraro-hyppolite, 13, from long island, new york, has an iq of 168. He scored 1,590 out of 1,600 on the sat at the age of 10 and earned his high school diploma at 11. He is currently working towards an undergraduate degree and plans to graduate in may 2027. His planned master's programme will focus on sports management.

Article Title: Maharashtra minister's niece Nila Vikhe Patil elected to Swedish Parliament
Article Text: Nila Vikhe Patil, daughter of Maharashtra educationist Ashok Vikhe Patil, was elected to the Swedish Parliament on Saturday from the Stockholm City constituency.Nila is the great-granddaughter of the founder of Asia’s first cooperative sugar factory, Vithalrao Vikhe Patil, and granddaughter of late Union minister Balasaheb Vikhe Patil. Her uncle, Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil, is a Maharashtra minister.Born in Sweden, Nila spent her early years in Ahmednagar, Maharashtra. She holds a bachelor’s degree and an MBA from the Gothenburg School of Business, with Economics and Law, and also studied for an MBA at the University of Complutense in Madrid.Since 2020, she has worked at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), a global services network, offering strategy, management, technology and risk consulting.In April 2025, she became an authorised public accountant.She has been a member of the Stockholm City Council. She also served as a political adviser in the Swedish Prime Minister’s Office, focusing on finance, taxes and housing during the Stefan Lofven administration.“It feels nice to be a part of the 349-member Parliament. I am looking forward to contributing to the city and the country,” Nila told news agency PTI.“I would like to be a voice for those who cannot vote,” she said. “I want to contribute to a society where every child gets a chance for a good future. We need a habitable planet with clean water, living nature and as few human-caused natural disasters as possible,” she added.The 41-year-old Nila said that she loves India dearly and misses her grandfather a lot.“I hope to make my grandfather proud. He made me read the state budget when I was 15,” Nila said.“I love India dearly and I feel very connected. I have lots of close Indian friends. I miss my grandfather a lot. He used to call me almost weekly during his last years,” she added.Sweden’s left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority in the September 13 election. The Swedish Election Authority said the four opposition parties won 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag (Parliament). The four parties that make up or support the outgoing conservative-led government took 173 seats.The opposition Green Party is focused on environmentalism, renewable energy and green politics.Nila has been active in the Green Party for 25 years and is a member of the Election Committee of the Stockholm Green Party.
Article Summary: Nila vikhe patil was elected to the swedish parliament on saturday. She is the great-granddaughter of the founder of asia’s first cooperative sugar factory. Nila spent her early years in ahmednagar, maharashtra. She has been active in the green party for 25 years.

Article Title: Smoke over Riyadh airport: Houthis launch major missile, drone attack on Saudi capital - video
Article Text:
The current round of fighting began in mid-July after strikes on Houthi-controlled Sanaa International Airport. The strikes came as an Iranian passenger plane carrying a senior Houthi delegation was returning from Iran.

Smoke seen near airport

Saudi Arabia says attacks were thwarted

Smoke rose near King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh after Yemen's Houthi rebels launched a large-scale attack on Saudi Arabia on Saturday. Two explosions were heard in the capital, while some flights were delayed.The Houthis said they targeted "sensitive targets" in Riyadh and a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu. The group said it used ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in the attacks.Saudi air defences later said they had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh.Videos showed a plume of smoke rising near King Khalid International Airport after the second explosion.Saudi authorities had earlier issued an aerial threat alert for Riyadh. They later announced that the danger had passed. The alert was reportedly the first such warning issued for the Saudi capital since tensions with the Houthis escalated.The Houthis reportedly targeted the fuel storage infrastructure at the airport triggering large plumes of smoke to rise up.There were no immediate reports of casualties or major damage in Riyadh.Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group had launched two major operations.The first targeted what he called "sensitive targets" in Riyadh. The second targeted a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu, a major industrial and energy hub on the Red Sea coast."The two operations were successful," Sarea said.He claimed that large fires broke out at the targeted sites. The claims could not be independently verified.The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted the missile targeting Riyadh. It also said attacks on Baish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu had been thwarted.Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said the attacks targeted "civilians and civilian objects". He also warned that Saudi Arabia would take "appropriate measures" to deter further attacks.The Houthis denied deliberately targeting civilians.Sarea said the attacks were in response to increased Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. He vowed to continue what he called an "escalation for escalation" strategy until Saudi airstrikes stop and restrictions on Yemen are lifted.The latest attack marks a major escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.The current round of fighting began in mid-July after strikes on Houthi-controlled Sanaa International Airport. The strikes came as an Iranian passenger plane carrying a senior Houthi delegation was returning from Iran.The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of being behind the strikes. They then launched missile and drone attacks in retaliation.On July 20, the group announced a ban on Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandab Strait. It has since claimed several attacks on Saudi tankers and oil facilities.
Article Summary: Houthi rebels launch large-scale attack on saudi arabia. Two explosions heard in the capital, while some flights are delayed. Houthis say they targeted "sensitive targets" in riyadh and a saudi aramco facility in yanbu. Saudi air defences say they intercepted and destroyed a houthi ballistic missile.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu on AI doom fears: ‘Without scientific scepticism, we risk being delusional’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

Sridhar Vembu says AI scepticism must stay grounded in science

James Maynard says he was wrong about AI predictions

Sridhar Vembu says conviction and scepticism both matter

Zoho founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu has shared his view on the growing debate over whether AI could pose serious risks to humanity. Sridhar Vembu said he has not bought into AI doom scenarios, but believes people should remain open to changing their views as AI models become more capable. Vembu was responding to a post by American physicist Steve Hsu, who shared comments from Fields Medalist James Maynard on X. Maynard said he had been sceptical of earlier AI predictions that sounded like science fiction but now takes the risks more seriously because many of those predictions have proved more accurate than he expected.Sridhar Vembu said people need both personal conviction and scientific scepticism when thinking about AI and its future.“I have not bought into the AI doom scenarios,” Vembu wrote on X, pointing to Maynard's changing position as an example of what he described as a scientific attitude.“Fields Medalist James Maynard teaches us the scientific attitude about this: he has been highly sceptical of claims of AI doom but as the models demonstrate higher and higher capability levels, he is taking them more seriously now.”Steve Hsu's post quoted Maynard discussing how his view of AI risks has changed.Maynard said he had followed AI for some time but had been sceptical of predictions that appeared to come from science fiction.“I've been interested and I've been following AI, but I've heard all these predictions that just sound like sci-fi and I've been consistently dismissive and skeptical of all of them.”He then acknowledged that his earlier view had been wrong.“But I've been consistently wrong. The people who sound like they're talking from a sci-fi novel are the people who've been making much much more accurate predictions.”Maynard concluded that AI risks should not simply be dismissed as hype.Vembu said personal conviction helps people continue working toward a goal, while scientific scepticism can prevent people from becoming disconnected from evidence.“Our own hunches and convictions allow us to pursue and stick to a course of action and scientific scepticism keeps us grounded in reality,” he wrote.He added:“Without a strong internal conviction, our actions lack the will power to succeed. Without scientific scepticism, we risk being delusional.”
Article Summary: Zoho founder and chief scientist sridhar vembu has shared his view on the growing debate over whether ai could pose serious risks to humanity. He was responding to a post by american physicist steve hsu, who shared comments from fields medalist james maynard on x. maynard said he had been sceptical of earlier ai predictions that sounded like science fiction.

Article Title: While most Americans may hate datacenters, UAE minister calls them 'more important than roads'; and has a new ‘hiding rule’ for them after war destroyed many
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Iran war changed how UAE deals with data centers 'forever'

'One country regulating AI will not work, it has to be almost the entire world'

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) will overhaul its regulatory framework for data centres and halt public disclosure of their physical locations to shield them from military threats, according to comments reported by The Next Web of a session from Salesforce's annual event Dreamforce 2026. Speaking alongside Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE’s Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, warned that computing hubs have evolved into critical infrastructure that requires heightened protection.Al Olama said that data centres have become prime targets because our whole lives exist on connected devices, arguing that they are now more important than bridges, roads, or tunnels. In remarks highlighted in the 'The Next Web' report, the minister stated that the UAE will no longer promote the locations of these facilities to prevent bad actors from targeting them, adding that he expects other nations will soon be forced to adopt similar measures. "Unfortunately they’re more important than bridges. They’re more important than roads. They’re more important than tunnels because our whole lives are on these devices that we’re using," said Al Olama, in a session Salesforce published.Incidentally, UAE minister's views are very different from that of most Americans. While Donald Trump government strongly supports data centres, most states across the US are not in strong favour of them. The debate around data center projects is one of the rare modern issues to cut across party lines, demographics and geography -- uniting the US. As a report in AP says, from Republican-dominated Nebraska, Texas and Wyoming to swing-state Pennsylvania to Democratic-leaning New Mexico, in a divided America, the left and right unite to oppose AI data centers.The strategic shift comes in the wake of severe regional conflict that began on February 28, a day Al Olama recalled preparing for a trip to Ecuador before hostilities escalated. The UAE faced more than 1,000 projectiles and drones during the first week of the conflict alone, with launches from Iran taking only two minutes to reach the country. Al Olama noted that the UAE intercepted more aerial threats than the entire Middle East and Israel combined, resulting in zero impact on human lives or business operations. Domestic life has since returned to normal, though the government is now decentralizing key digital assets, including splitting up its domestic Stargate data centre project and investing in offshore facilities, such as in Germany.Reflecting on broader AI policy, Al Olama warned against allowing fear to choke innovation, drawing a historical parallel to the Middle East’s technological decline after centuries of dominance from 813 to 1515 AD. That era ended when the region banned the Gutenberg printing press for two centuries due to fears over misinformation, alterations to holy scripture, and general administrative anxiety. He cautioned that modern leaders cannot afford to repeat that mistake with artificial intelligence, even if the technology's rapid evolution initially seems frightening.When it comes to public deployment, Al Olama advocated a measured approach that avoids unproven, high-risk systems. UAE public services, such as Abu Dhabi’s TAMM administrative platform, run on established, older large language models rather than cutting-edge frontier systems like OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Fable, which he warned carry significant cybersecurity and data breach risks. He also drew hard red lines against using AI for predictive policing, citing the danger of false positives, and cautioned against building an oppressive surveillance apparatus, pointing instead to quality-of-life improvements like desk-free biometric airport transit.To insulate the domestic workforce from technological displacement, the UAE has trained all 80,000 federal civil servants in agentic AI, following an earlier initiative that taught prompt design to one million people. Al Olama dismissed fears of mass unemployment, insisting the technology will ultimately create opportunities and boost workforce capability.Addressing the global regulatory landscape, Al Olama noted that governments typically overregulate while the private sector tends to underregulate. He pointed to the UAE’s own data protection laws, which were initially drafted by tech companies before state officials and civil society refined them, as a model for collaborative oversight. He warned Western policymakers that unilateral bans on AI would simply hand an insurmountable advantage to competitors, arguing that restrictions in the United States make little sense unless China agrees to follow suit.
Article Summary: Omar sultan al olama, the uae’s minister of state for artificial intelligence, digital economy and remote work applications, warned that computing hubs have evolved into critical infrastructure that require heightened protection. He said the uae will no longer promote the locations of these facilities to prevent bad actors from targeting them.
